blocks.text: It is Merops apiaster Linn. (T. 1, vol. 1, p. 460, ed. Gmelin), of which, however, there is more than one species. Forsskål in Descriptt. Animall. p. 1 mentions two. 1. Merops Aegyptius, entirely green, with a yellow throat, a black line along the sides of the head, and the flight feathers dusky at the tip. Arab. Chaddaeir [a word to be written in Arabic letters as خضير [khḍyr]]. 2. Merops, Arab. Schaeghagha, شغاق [shghāq] (the same word as شقراق [shqrāq], but written according to the popular pronunciation), to which name Forsskål added this: "It agrees exactly with Merops Apiaster Linn.; but the bill is not keeled but convex, and the toes are not joined at the lowest joint. Locality: Temen, frequent in the woods; it feeds on insects." There is a further species, described by Hasselquist in his Travels, p. 302 f., under the name merops galilaeus, whose Arabic name he says is Varvar; this very word appears in Golius' Lex. Arab., p. 2650, under the root وَرْوَرَ [warwara], he sharpened: "وَرْوَارٌ [warwārun] merops [bee-eater], from its sharp bill." Compare what Oedmann has on this [III, 50] bird, Fasc. 1, Chapter 5, p. 73–75. He thinks it is the same as the Corvus Aegyptius, green and spotted, with the middle of the back blue, described by Hasselquist, p. 296 f. But when Oedmann asserts that the Arabs write that the شقراق [shqrāq] is a harbinger of rain, that very learned man is mistaken. Certainly the Arabs whom Bochart excerpted in this place say nothing of the kind.
